newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer says Euro must earn stability reputation.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says Euro must earn stability reputation.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday that the future single European currency would not automatically be stable against the dollar and would have to earn its reputation.

"The European central bank must earn this reputation (for stability)," Tietmeyer said in the text of a speech for a reception sponsored by German vehicle maker Mercedes-Benz AG at the IAA truck exhibition in Hanover.
"That can under the circumstances take a while because credibility can mostly not be built overnight," he said.
Tietmeyer also said he hoped the new currency, to be called the Euro and which is slated for launch in January 1999, would not fluctuate against the yen and dollar as much as the mark currently does.
"There is the hope that the Euro will not fluctuate as much as the mark," Tietmeyer said in the speech.
"How far this hope will be fulfilled is hard to predict," he added, noting that the stability of the new currency will be pegged to solid monetary and fiscal policies.
In addition, he again pushed for a detailed stability pact to secure public budgets once the new currency is launched.

European officials meeting in Dublin at the weekend cleared key hurdles in their quest for a stability pact to control public spending once countries enter monetary union, but failed to agree exactly how the deal will work.
"It cannot be allowed that, after the start of currency union, countries put their feet up on the table in terms of stability policies because of the lack of effective sanctions," Tietmeyer said.
Referring to the results of the Dublin meeting, Tietmeyer said: "There are still a few important questions left open."
Tietmeyer warned that fiscal criteria for entry into currency union should not be seen as less important than other requirements set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
"One should not say that the fiscal criteria should be less important. Experience shows that sooner or later slack finances endanger monetary policy," Tietmeyer said.
"That also applies for currency union. If anything, price stability lends itself to yet higher interest rates," he said.
Tietmeyer also said German companies would have the least to win in terms of interest rates with the new currency.
He said that the earlier privilege of having their home currency viewed as a reserve currency would be lost against competitors from currency member countries.
